title: Hybridization of Neural Networks and Numerical Solvers in JAX with Differentiable Physics
description:
This is the lecture I gave at the ML & AD for Scientific Computing in JAX workshop at Strasbourg in June 2026. All the material can be found here: https://github.com/Ceyron/hybridization-in-jax

What the talk covers:
- Numerical simulators and neural networks side by side: compute graphs, autodiff
  granularity (scalar / BLAS / algebra / whole-operation), and what actually differs
- A deliberately strict definition of hybridization, and why PINNs, Neural ODEs,
  Hamiltonian/Lagrangian NNs and Deep Equilibrium Models don't fall under it
- The spectrum of learned components: full surrogate → full-field correction →
  embedded networks → calibration and data assimilation → classical numerics
- Why hybridization helps
- What it costs: non-smooth operations, implicit differentiation through linear
  solves, and the very pragmatic problem of a legacy Fortran solver on a CPU
- Backpropagation through time as both curse and blessing: gradient cuts, the
  O(1)-memory reversibility trick and why it usually fails, checkpointing, and
  progressively refined differentiable physics
- Case studies: Solver-in-the-loop and ML-accelerated CFD
- Preparation for the practical session

---

Here are all the references I used in the lecture:

1) https://fkoehler.site/autodiff-table/
A collection of primitive rules for explicit autodiff (i.e., the atomic library you would approximately find within JAX).

2) https://fkoehler.site/implicit-autodiff-table/
A collection of autodiff primitive rules when using implicit autodiff (like over linear or nonlinear solves).

3) https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.00180
APEBench, a benchmark I published at NeurIPS 2024, where, among other things, we empirically show the relationship between numerical solvers and neural emulators.

4) https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.07366  https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.01563  https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.04630
Neural ODEs, Hamiltonian Neural Networks, and Lagrangian Neural Networks: a collection of ways to learn the RHS or the energy/Hamiltonian of a system. All of it makes cool usage of autodiff.

5) https://fkoehler.site/corrector-configurations/
A collection of all the ways one could couple neural networks and coarse solvers in a correction layout, i.e., the compute graph spawned by these two components in different setups.

6) https://fkoehler.site/predictor-learning-setups
A large collection of SVG schematics of how one can train autoregressive emulators (and neural-hybrid correctors) by changing the handling of time, reference, as well as modifications to the backward pass.

7) https://ipc-sim.github.io/
A popular technique in computer graphics and structural mechanics simulations to enable fast detection and resolution of contacts (In the lecture, I used the example of contact mechanics for its high nonlinearity, even discontinuity, as a potential challenging case for naive autodiff).

8) https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.08824v1
SoftJAX is a new library that provides softened modifications of classically non-differentiable operations in JAX.

9) https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.15183
A study and a JAX library of how to enable automatic handling of implicit conditions in autodiff by using implicit differentiation and employing matrix-free linear solvers for the derivative propagation.

10) https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.12971
How to build neural-hybrid correctors without a differentiable simulator by cleverly cutting the backpropagation-through-time.

11) https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.19611
How to reduce the cost of training neural-hybrid correctors by scheduling the fidelity of the coarse simulator.

12) https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.00016
Seminal work on how to build neural-hybrid correctors in the "slap-on the NN" deep-learning native way.

13) https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.01010
Highly influential work on how a neural-hybrid corrector can achieve significant speedups over a coarser classical numerical simulator.

title: Full Lyapunov Spectrum of Chaotic Lorenz System using JAX
description:
The largest Lyapunov exponent indicates the presence of deterministic chaos in a dynamical system. Additionally, more interesting properties of a system can be deduced from an entire Lyapunov spectrum, e.g., the Kaplan-Yorke dimension describing the fractal structure. Let's approximate the full spectrum via pushing orthonormal matrix variations through the integration on the chaotic attractor. We will derive the integrator's Jacobian using JAX's automatic differentiation engine. description: In this video I will explain a very interesting concept called Local Intrinsic Dimension (LID) which actually shapes a good part of the Machine Learning and AI fields. Low LID means more structured, less noisy, easier to learn data. Thus it is a measure of data complexity specifically when we use algorithms that work on local regions like KNN, and Decision Trees. PCA is another one. Although it reduces the Intrinsic Dimension globally, still is very relevant to the topic.

title: All sparse models are wrong, but some are useful
description:
Sparse Principal Component Analysis (Sparse PCA or SPCA) is an extension of the classic Principal Component Analysis (PCA) used for dimensionality reduction and multivariate data analysis. Its key distinction is that it introduces a sparsity structure to the principal components (PCs) for reasons of simplicity and interpretability. For instance, in genetics (gene expression data), a sparse PC might only involve a few specific genes, allowing researchers to focus their follow-up analysis on those key genes. In this presentation, I will discuss theoretical properties that can make the variable selection in SPCA unreliable or non-unique, how to understand this problem and avoid misinterpretation.

title: Probabilistic Tensor Decomposition
description: The vast majority of tensor decomposition methods are based on least squares estimation - or equivalent maximum likelihood under a Gaussian distribution. Importantly, the probabilistic tensor decomposition methods are more robust to noise and model misspecification, provides new strategies for determining the right number of components, and in-build tools for characterizing model uncertainty. title: Semi-Automated Machine Learning for Calibration Model Development
description:
Manuel A. Palacios and Barry M. Wise from Eigenvector Research talk about the very intriguing Diviner.

The story: AutoML, or Automated Machine Learning, represents a paradigm where the entire pipeline of data preprocessing, variable selection, feature engineering, model selection, and hyperparameter tuning is automated, typically leading to a singular optimized model. While highly efficient and simple from the end-user perspective, this approach often lacks transparency and customizability. Furthermore, the black-box nature of AutoML might overlook models that an analyst would have preferred, instead prioritizing what it deems the 'best' model, potentially missing nuanced solutions tailored to specific needs.

In this talk we introduce Diviner, (from Divine—to discover or locate something by intuition, insight or supernatural means), a novel semi-autoML approach that transcends the traditional black-box model by actively involving the analyst in the model-building process. Unlike conventional autoML methods that yield a single optimal model, our approach creates a family of models and ranks them by their cross-validation performance, degree of overfitting, and prediction error on validation sets. 

Diviner commences with user-assisted outlier assessment via Principal Components Analysis (PCA) and Robust Partial Least Squares (RPLS), followed by variable selection to hone significant predictors. Various data-relevant preprocessing algorithms are explored, and linear models (Partial Least Squares and Elastic Net) are calibrated (with hyperparameter tuning) and ranked. At this point, the end-user selects the models to keep and take for further refinement, including re-assessment of outliers, preprocessing and variable selection fine-tuning. Finally, the user chooses the models to output. This can be a single model, a series of the top-ranked models, or an ensemble of models which can be further optimized.

Diviner bridges the gap between full automation and user-led customization, leading to more insightful and transparent model-building. Through the evaluation of several datasets, we demonstrate promising results in predictive accuracy and model diversity. This research not only contributes to the practical application of autoML but also sparks a dialogue on rethinking how autoML models are constructed, evaluated, and understood, moving away from the black-box solution to a more collaborative, interpretable, and adaptive methodology.

title: Monday Webinar: Causal latent space-based models in the Quality by Design paradigm
description:
Latent variable-based models, such as Partial Least Squares (PLS), are essential tools in the Quality by Design (QbD) paradigm, enabling the analysis of highly correlated datasets, typical of Industry 4.0, while preserving causal relationships in the reduced latent space. Aligned with the QbD initiative, this webinar presents a latent variable-based approach to define the raw material design space (i.e., raw material specifications) that ensures quality assurance with a given confidence level for Critical Quality Attributes (CQAs). Additionally, an effective process control system attenuating most raw material variations is implemented by manipulating process variables. A novel latent space-based multivariate capability index is also introduced to rank raw material suppliers, establishing a direct link between raw material properties and CQAs. This index facilitates supplier selection before manufacturing a single unit of the product, enhancing decision-making in quality management.

title: Three-way data reduction based on essential information - Monday webinar
description:
In the domain of bilinear curve resolution, the identification and extraction of essential information from sets of multivariate measurements has recently garnered significant attention primarily in the light of the fact that such an approach is capable of compressing the data at hand while preserving their local rank properties and, thus, enabling their accurate factorisation in a dramatically shorter amount of time. In this presentation, the idea of essential information-based data reduction is extended to trilinear datasets through the description of an original algorithmic procedure leveraging the principles of Higher Order Singular Value Decomposition (HOSVD). The performance of this novel algorithm will be evaluated in both real-world and simulated scenarios which will permit to highlight the benefits it can bring in domains like multiway fluorescence spectroscopy and imaging.
This work was conducted in collaboration with Azar Azizi (University of Sistan and Baluchestan, Zahedan, Iran), Nematollah Omidikia (University of Sistan and Baluchestan, Zahedan, Iran), Mahdiyeh Ghaffari (Radboud University, Nijmegen, The Netherlands), and Cyril Ruckebusch (Université de Lille, Lille, France).

Make Your Coding Agents Way Faster (Jev + Google Antigravity)
description:
Explore Voice AI agents: https://morak.ai

Standard LLMs are great for writing text, but token-by-token generation introduces major latency when running high-frequency agent loops. 

In this video, I'll show you how to harness Jev—a specialized classification model built for sub-50ms non-text decisions—inside coding agents like Google Antigravity, Claude Code, and Codex. I break down how Jev bypasses text parsing to return typed values, explore its three core primitives (Choice, Score, and Noul), and look at community projects like Gregor Zuni's 7.1-second Google Flights automation. Finally, I jump into Google Antigravity to install the TypeSafe skill and build a live model router that automatically delegates tasks to Gemini Flash or Gemini Pro based on complexity.

2. It handles structured classification perfectly but is not built for text generation, math, or counting.
3. Jev uses literal evaluation, so write explicit descriptions and filter your state data rather than dumping giant contexts into the prompt.

title: World Building: How 3D Gaussian Splatting is Transforming Digital Twins
description:
We have expertise across all aspects of the 3DGS pipeline. Contact the SEI if you’d like support adopting this technology: info@sei.cmu.edu  

Creating high-fidelity digital twins has traditionally been costly and time consuming. A new class of volumetric modeling techniques is changing this paradigm by enabling the creation of photorealistic visual models and geometrically accurate 3D meshes from real-world data. In this webcast, we will explore one emerging approach—3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)—and discuss how organizations can leverage these models for applications such as simulation, training, visualization, autonomous systems, and digital engineering.

Attendees will learn 
• how contemporary approaches are enabling faster, more scalable creation of digital twins
• the fundamentals of 3D Gaussian Splatting and practical considerations for using the technology
• how organizations can apply 3DGS-based models to support mission, engineering, and operational needs 

#3dgs #gaussiansplatting #digitaltwins @TheSEICMU

Introduction and Welcome: (0:00 - 2:42) Shane McGraw introduces speakers Matthew Walsh and Dominic Ross from the Software Engineering Institute.

Why Create Digital Replicas?: (2:43 - 8:08) The speakers discuss the utility of creating digital copies of the physical world for training, reconnaissance, and space manipulation.

Understanding 3D Gaussian Splatting: (8:09 - 15:25) An overview of the 3DGS pipeline, including Structure from Motion (SfM) and fitting Gaussians for photorealistic rendering.

Practical Pipeline Implementation: (15:26 - 24:26) A detailed look at the SEI war-fighter-centered pipeline, including deployable kits for object capture and mobile rigs for scene capture.

Applications and Use Cases: (24:27 - 47:49) Examples of leveraging 3DGS models, including Calamityville reconstruction for active shooter training and maintenance training for aircraft parts.

Data Collection Best Practices: (47:50 - 55:00) Tips for data acquisition, such as using consistent lighting and planning scan paths.

Key Takeaways and Conclusion: (55:01 - 1:00:26) Summary of 3DGS as a mature, accessible technology for organizations to leverage today.

title: Intro to the SEI CERT Coding Standard for Fortran
description:
SEI CERT Fortran Coding Standard
https://cmu-sei.github.io/secure-coding-standards/sei-cert-fortran-coding-standard

Fortran is one of the oldest high-level programming languages still in active use and remains a cornerstone of scientific, engineering, and high-performance computing (HPC) software in critical applications areas, such as climate and weather prediction, aerospace, nuclear energy, computational physics, and national security. Fortran provides several features that are particularly well-suited for scientific and high-performance computing, including intrinsic multidimensional array operations, native array slicing and whole-array syntax, built-in support for numerical computation, explicit parallel programming constructs, and language-level facilities for efficient vectorization and mathematical optimization. Recently, the Fortran community has shown growing interest in secure software development practices, vulnerability prevention, and secure coding standards. The SEI CERT Coding Standard for Fortran leverages expertise in secure coding practices and provides well-documented and enforceable coding guidelines to audit Fortran software. 

Attendees will learn how to

• identify common security risks in Fortran
• navigate the SEI CERT Coding Standard for Fortran
• leverage Fortran safety features for secure coding
• improve software quality through secure coding practices

Subsea cables are high-capacity fiber-optic lines laid along the ocean floor to enable global communication by transmitting data between continents. Spanning thousands of miles, they carry an estimated 95% of international internet, phone, and data transmissions.

Critically, these cables are vulnerable to sabotage by state actors, as they form critical infrastructure for global communication and economic stability. Indeed, Russia and China have been implicated in activities targeting subsea cables as recently as November 2024, and experts warn that these networks are likely to be focal points in future conflicts, heightening geopolitical tensions.

Josh Dzieza is a reporter for The Verge and has covered the subsea cable industry and the strategic importance of subsea cables. He joins the podcast alongside Gregor Vand to discuss this invisible, and increasingly important, network infrastructure.

The Armorr GamersBox basically turns your console into a portable gaming setup by putting it inside a rugged case with a built-in 21.5-inch display. I tested it with my PS5 to find out how well it actually works, how tough it really is, and whether a $400 case like this makes sense.

I tested the display, speakers, portability, console temperatures, and even stood on the GamersBox to put its durability claims to the test. I also spent time actually gaming on it with Spider-Man 2 and compared the display side-by-side with a traditional gaming monitor.

There are definitely some compromises here. You’re getting a 1080p 75Hz display rather than a high-refresh gaming monitor, and I found a few design details I’d like to see improved. But after actually traveling around with consoles before, I can also see a very specific type of gamer getting a lot of use out of something like this.

So who is the GamersBox actually for, and is it worth around $400? That’s what I wanted to find out.
